blocks.text: INNNEWS - as an ideological nationalist party, the PDI-P faces a dilemma when antiWestern narrative promotes sympathy towards Iran, while reality within Iran shows a repression pattern that's hard to ignore.

There's a paradox that is increasingly visible in Indonesian political dynamics. As an idealistic party of nationalism and pluralism, the PDIP seems to be dragged into a global narrative that simplifies reality. In this context, Iran is no longer read as a country with its internal complexity, but as a symbol of the Western resistance.

The object of that symbol is Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and the system he's leading. Ever since the Iranian Revolution, Iran has built a very central power structure on religious authorities that have not been selected directly, with the consequences of political opposition and civil liberties. But in a particular narrative, this aspect becomes secondary. The prominent one is the position of an actor who dares challenge Western hegemonies.
This is where the illusion lies.

In a framed global order, perceptions often transcend reality. Narasi anti- imperialism, which does have a strong historical root in Indonesian political identity, creates easily translated resonance into sympathy against those who are considered to be fighting. But this resonance is not always followed by consistent moral evaluations.

For some in PDI-P orbits, Iran became a symbolic instrument in the sovereignty and resistance talks. But when symbols replace substance, there are more serious risks. The ideological nationalism that should be rooted in the sovereignty of the people and pluralism is potentially slipping into radicalism romanticism, where resistance is rewarded not because of its moral value, but simply because of its opposite position with the West.
The consequences are the cover-up of reality.

In Iran, a repression pattern of religious minors, including the Christian community, shows another face of the system. The church speaks Persians are restricted, religious activities in local languages are suspected of being a threat, and many Christians, especially those who have moved faith, facing arrest and imprisonment on the charge of national security. The house ceremony was disbanded, the leader was detained, and religious activities were closely watched.

Conversion to Kristen is not legally recognized, which leaves the bride without legal protection. Pressure presents not only socially, but also administrative and structural. In a system like this, personal faith can be easily polyitized as an ideological threat.
Ignoring this reality would mean sacrificing moral consistency.

This simplification phenomenon isn't just happening in Indonesia. globally, countries are often reduced to black-and-white images, heroes or criminals, depending on their position in international power. In a skeleton like this, complexity is considered irrelevant, even disturbing.
But that's exactly where the danger is.

When human rights abuses are selectively assessed, the principle loses its power. When the symbol is more dominant than fact, political judgment becomes hazy. And when global narratives are imported without filtering, the ideological identity of a nation can be distorted.

Indonesia is not Iran. Pancasila rejects the unification of absolute religious authority to state rule. Indonesia's democracy, with all its limitations, was built on pluralism and institutional balance. In this context, the uncritical sympathy for power models like Iran becomes contradictory with that foundation.

For PDI-P, the challenge was not simply to preserve antiWestern narratives, but to maintain ideological consistency. A healthy nationalism not only talks about sovereignty, but also about moral integrity in judging anyone, without double standard.
Resistance is not automatic moral. Its value is determined by what is fought and what is built instead.
If the symbol continues to replace reality, then what's left is not analysis, but illusion. And in politics, illusions that are left too long can turn into expensive strategic mistakes.
Author:
Doctor. Hanny semanaga, M.B.A.
General Chairman
Indonesian Fornak
Christian Nationalism Forum
